content.text:
Looking at the cyan cells, I notice column 5 has five of them (rows 3-7), forming a vertical line, and the diagonal r-c=0 also has four cells covering rows 3,4,6,7. I'm checking whether these two lines together cover every cyan cell.

Now I'm mapping out the remaining 7-valued cells and 1-valued cell to figure out the symmetry group generated by the vertical reflection (c → 10-c) and the diagonal swap (r,c → c,r). Together these two reflections generate the full dihedral group of order 8 for the 11×11 grid, meaning every non-cyan cell's orbit consists of up to 8 symmetric positions. I'm computing the orbit of (1,2) under this group by applying identity, vertical reflection, diagonal swap, and horizontal reflection to see all its images.

Orbit of (1,9) collapses to {(1,9),(1,1),(9,1),(9,9)}, colored 1. Orbit of (1,4) includes (1,6),(9,4),(9,6),(4,1),(4,9),(6,1),(6,9), all matching color 7. The remaining points I check — (4,1),(6,1),(7,9),(8,1),(9,3),(9,4) — all fall into orbits I've already resolved, confirming their colors.

Now I'm building the output grid, starting from all zeros and placing the cyan cells at (3,3),(3,5),(4,4),(4,5),(5,5),(6,5),(6,6),(7,5),(7,7), noting these don't overlap with any orbit cells. I list out the three symmetric orbits colored 7: one covering positions like (1,2),(1,8),(9,2),(9,8),(2,1),(2,9),(8,1),(8,9), another covering (1,3),(1,7),(9,3),(9,7),(3,1),(3,9),(7,1),(7,9), and the third covering (1,4),(1,6),(9,4),(9,6),(4,1

Row8 finishes with c9=7, row9 mirrors row1's pattern with 1,7,7,7,0,7,7,7,1, and row10 is all zeros.
